content.text: Now, let's explore the four main types of chemical reactions.

scenes.teacherScript: Now that we know how to balance equations, let's explore the four main types of chemical reactions you will see in chemistry.

content.description: Two or more reactants combine to form a single product.

scenes.teacherScript: First is the Combination Reaction. Here, two or more reactants combine to form a single product. Let's look at this beaker. We have Calcium Oxide, also known as quicklime. When we add water, it reacts vigorously to form Calcium Hydroxide, or slaked lime. See that red glow? A large amount of heat is evolved! Reactions where heat is released are called Exothermic reactions.

Here is the chemical equation: CaO solid plus H2O liquid gives Ca(OH)2 aqueous, plus heat. Fun fact: A solution of this slaked lime is used for whitewashing walls! It slowly reacts with carbon dioxide in the air to form a shiny layer of Calcium Carbonate.

The opposite of combination is the Decomposition Reaction. In this reaction, a single reactant breaks down into simpler products. This usually requires energy in the form of heat, light, or electricity. Reactions that absorb energy are called Endothermic reactions.

content.heading: Activity 1.5: Heating Ferrous Sulphate
bullets: Heat green ferrous sulphate crystals in a boiling tube.
The green colour changes to brown.
A characteristic odour of burning sulphur is emitted.

scenes.teacherScript: Let's perform an activity. Take about 2 grams of green ferrous sulphate crystals in a boiling tube and heat it over a flame. You'll observe the green colour changing to brown, and you'll smell the characteristic odour of burning sulphur!

When decomposition is carried out by heating, it's called Thermal Decomposition. For example, heating green Ferrous Sulphate crystals produces solid brown Ferric Oxide, and emits sulphur dioxide and sulphur trioxide gases. You can actually smell the burning sulphur!

content.heading: Activity 1.6: Heating Lead Nitrate
bullets: Heat lead nitrate powder in a boiling tube.
These fumes are nitrogen dioxide gas.

scenes.teacherScript: Here is another experiment. If you hold a boiling tube containing lead nitrate powder over a flame, you will observe the emission of thick brown fumes. These fumes are nitrogen dioxide gas.
Another important thermal decomposition is heating Lead Nitrate powder. It produces Lead Oxide, Oxygen, and distinct brown fumes of Nitrogen Dioxide gas.

content.description: Electric current decomposes water into Hydrogen and Oxygen gases.

scenes.teacherScript: Decomposition can also happen via electricity! This is called Electrolytic Decomposition. When we pass an electric current through water, it decomposes into Hydrogen and Oxygen gases. Notice how there is twice as much Hydrogen gas bubbling up as Oxygen. That's because water is H2O!

content.heading: Activity 1.8: Sunlight on Silver Chloride
bullets: Place white silver chloride in a china dish.
Leave it in sunlight for some time.

scenes.teacherScript: Let's look at one more activity. Take some white silver chloride powder in a china dish and place it in sunlight. After some time, you'll see the white powder turning grey. Why does this happen?

content.heading: Photolytic Decomposition
bullets: White Silver Chloride turns grey in sunlight.
Used in black and white photography.

scenes.teacherScript: Finally, we have Photolytic Decomposition, caused by light. If you place white Silver Chloride in sunlight, it turns grey because it decomposes into silver and chlorine. This reaction is famously used in black and white photography!

content.description: A more reactive element displaces a less reactive one.

scenes.teacherScript: Moving on to our third type: Displacement Reaction. A more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound. Let's drop some iron nails into a blue copper sulphate solution. After a while, the nails get a brown coating of copper, and the solution turns green because iron sulphate is formed. Iron has displaced the copper!

content.heading: Activity 1.10: Double Displacement Reaction
bullets: Exchange of ions between the reactants.
Example: Sodium Sulphate + Barium Chloride -> Barium Sulphate precipitate.
Often produces an insoluble substance called a precipitate.

scenes.teacherScript: Our final type is the Double Displacement Reaction. Here, there is an exchange of ions between the reactants. When we mix solutions of Sodium Sulphate and Barium Chloride, a white, insoluble substance called Barium Sulphate is formed. This insoluble solid is called a precipitate, so these are also known as Precipitation reactions.
The equation is Na2SO4 plus BaCl2 gives BaSO4 solid precipitate plus 2NaCl.
